transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-29 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Lin (Redwood AE), Ravi Singh (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendes (Ventus Infra Lead), Aisha Farouk (Ventus ML Platform), Tom Becker (Ventus CTO)

Summary:
Quick deep dive into repeated GPU eviction/timeouts observed in Ventus's private deployment. Primary hypotheses: prefetch/pinned memory behavior combined with background heartbeat causing spikes; potential CUDA driver timestamps and soft OOM leading to watch-dog resets. Agreed to run targeted reproducer with prefetch toggles and enhanced logging.

Topics: Prefetch behavior, KV cache warmup, batching profile, watchdog/heartbeat, CUDA timeout patterns, retry semantics, on-prem network isolated (VPC) specifics.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya Lin: ok, hi everyone thanks for hopping on. this is Maya from Redwood. uh Ravi is here, our SE, and on the Ventus side we've got Carlos, Aisha, Tom. quick agenda, reproduce, root cause hypotheses, and next steps. sound good?
[00:15] Carlos Mendes: yep that's right. We're seeing intermittent evictions on our on-prem boxes, mostly during high-concurrency bursts. sometimes the worker restarts, sometimes we just get a timeout and the request 404s out.
[00:28] Ravi Singh: can you describe the hardware and the driver stack? like GPU model, driver, cuda, nvidia multiprocess server or anything like that?
[00:35] Aisha Farouk: sure, we're on p4-ish equiv boxes, actually they're A40 class. driver is Nvidia 520.xx, cuda 12.2. it's a bare-metal cluster behind a VPC peering and we've got Redwood Private running inside the VPC.
[00:52] Tom Becker: and just to add, the issue seems more common when our team runs batched inference with a long prompt set — like 2k tokens — and we do bursts of concurrent sessions during business hours.
[01:05] Ravi Singh: ok. two initial suspect areas — one is prefetch and async DMA into pinned memory which can temporarily spike GPU memory and cause soft oom/eviction. the other is watchdog timeouts: if a CUDA launch takes longer than the driver watchdog threshold, host will reset the context.
[01:24] Carlos Mendes: we see logs mentioning cudaErrorLaunchTimeout or just generic device reset in syslogs. sometimes the runtime logs show kvcache fetches taking 50-100ms unexpectedly.
[01:36] Maya Lin: when you say kvcache fetches, is that during generation for long context windows? are you seeing repeated misses and then big prefetch reads?
[01:44] Aisha Farouk: yes, misses then a ton of reads. our workload tends to pin a lot of kv around 1.5GB per request for the longer prompts. when concurrency is 8–12 we push the each-GPU memory to the edge.
[01:57] Ravi Singh: that aligns with a pattern we've seen where the runtime will prefetch full attention blocks for new sequences which temporarily doubles working set while prefetch completes. if the driver is older it might not handle the burst well and the watchdog trips.
[02:12] Tom Becker: is prefetch something we can turn off at runtime? we rely on it for latency but if it kills stability we might prefer slightly higher latency but no evictions.
[02:20] Ravi Singh: yes, we expose a runtime flag. there's also a tuned path where we stream KV in smaller chunks — that reduces peak memory but cost same latency in many cases. we'll test toggles.
[02:31] Carlos Mendes: also, sometimes after restart the model warmup fails and we see heavy regen and more OOMs. it cascades, like restart -> cold KV -> bulk prefetch -> eviction again.
[02:42] Maya Lin: that's an important cascade. so there's a warmup/kvcache priming window and if that coincides with new big batches it's a bad signal. we should look at pinned memory allocations and whether the allocator fragments.
[02:53] Ravi Singh: fragmentation's a thing. on older CUDA, cudaMalloc/cudaFree churn can fragment the device heap. one mitigation is to use a caching allocator (we do) but also to avoid large synchronous prefetches. alternative is offloading part of KV to host pinned memory — more PCIe traffic but lower device footprint.
[03:10] Aisha Farouk: but our infra team worries about PCIe saturation; we do have a limited PCIe lane setup on these boards.
[03:18] Tom Becker: also curious about watchdog config; in on-prem we can tune the driver watchdog but that's often risky for other apps on node. any runtime-level watchdog or soft-timeout an option?
[03:28] Ravi Singh: we have graceful fallback logic — for long kernels we can split execution into smaller ops and yield back to host between chunks. that trades some latency but avoids hitting the driver's two-second watchdog in many cases.
[03:40] Carlos Mendes: do you have any instrumentation we can enable to see per-kernel runtime histograms? our logs only show aggregated token times.
[03:48] Ravi Singh: yes, we'll enable verbose kernel timings in the runtime and emit per-kernel histograms and cuda stream queue lengths. we'll also collect nvprof-like traces if we need deeper analysis.
[03:58] Maya Lin: for reproducer, Ravi, can you outline the exact steps you'll run so Carlos can run same on staging? the goal is to get a deterministic failure within an hour ideally.
[04:07] Ravi Singh: plan — baseline: run current config with current batch sizes and token lengths for 30 minutes with background synthetic traffic to simulate production. step two: turn off prefetch and run same load. step three: enable chunked-kv streaming and re-run. collect dmesg, nvidia-smi dmon, runtime logs with kernel timings, and driver logs. I'll share a script.
[04:26] Aisha Farouk: sounds good. what's the expectation for log size? we have limited retention on the nodes.
[04:33] Ravi Singh: we'll make the script rotate logs and only keep a compressed tarball of the minute ranges around any device resets. should be manageable.
[04:40] Carlos Mendes: ok. another data point — we've noticed timeouts correlate with certain input patterns: long nested bullet lists and code blocks (from customers doing code gen). could prompt shape affect kv locality?
[04:52] Ravi Singh: absolutely. dense attention (many tokens with high attention fan-out) causes more KV traffic. quantization choices also matter — with int8 kernels you sometimes increase compute bursts, which lengthen kernel time and can hit watchdog.
[05:04] Tom Becker: are there recommended quantization profiles that avoid these bursts? we tried q8_0 and saw slightly faster throughput but more instability.
[05:12] Ravi Singh: q8_0 tends to have more aggressive packing; q4 or mixed precision is often more stable. we can suggest a profile tuned for your sequence length distribution. part of Redwood Optimize's recommendations but we'll give an immediate suggestion.
[05:25] Maya Lin: diving into network-on-prem specifics — you mentioned VPC peering and isolation. any chance the heartbeat traffic between control plane and nodes is getting delayed and leading the runtime to think a node is dead, triggering restarts?
[05:36] Carlos Mendes: control plane comms are internal and usually fine; we do see occasional net spikes during backups. if the heartbeat misses multiple times the runtime's failover will try to reassign, causing double-inits.
[05:47] Ravi Singh: we can tune heartbeat retries and make failover more conservative under heavy prefetch/warmup. also enabling 'graceful fail' so that a node that misses heartbeats keeps serving existing sessions until full timeout would help.
[05:57] Aisha Farouk: that seems promising. any downside? it might delay detection of truly dead nodes.
[06:02] Ravi Singh: tradeoff, yes. we can couple detection with liveness checks (GPU health) rather than pure network heartbeats.
[06:09] Tom Becker: OK, what about retry semantics — if a request fails with a CUDA timeout, what's Redwood's default? immediate retry? backoff?
[06:17] Maya Lin: default is one immediate retry to a cold model on a different node, then exponential backoff. but that can increase load if many requests get retried simultaneously.
[06:27] Ravi Singh: for these cases we'll recommend jittered backoff and prefer requeueing in the request broker rather than immediate second attempt. also fall back to a lighter quantized model for quick response if allowed by SLOs.
[06:39] Carlos Mendes: are there options to pin critical customers to dedicated capacity to avoid noisy neighbor problems?
[06:44] Maya Lin: yes that's Redwood Dedicated; you can reserve GPU pools or configure soft isolation. we can scope cost impact if Ventus wants to pilot.
[06:54] Aisha Farouk: back to repro — please include env vars we should set to reproduce allocator behavior.
[06:59] Ravi Singh: I'll include MALLOC_ARENA and our runtime caching allocator flags; also set CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=0 to keep async behavior. we'll record with CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1 for a couple runs to correlate kernel ordering.
[07:12] Carlos Mendes: thanks. one more note — after evictions we saw device memory leak that required a node reboot to reclaim fully. that suggests fragmentation plus driver leak.
[07:21] Ravi Singh: yep could be driver bug. collecting driver logs and kernel traces will help. if it's a reproducible driver leak we'll work with NVIDIA and recommend patching or driver rollback/test.
[07:31] Maya Lin: ok let's recap next steps and owners.
[07:35] Carlos Mendes: quick question — do you have prebuilt scripts we can run or do we need to build from source?
[07:40] Ravi Singh: we'll provide a tarball with the reproducer that uses the Redwood runtime debug binary — no build required — and a small harness to simulate traffic. you'll need to run as root or with sudo to capture dmesg and driver logs.
[07:52] Tom Becker: fine. we can try to run this tomorrow and will prioritize the staging cluster.
[07:58] Maya Lin: great. thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the script and schedule a 30-minute follow-up mid next week.
